about: What the CipherHorizon inventory scripts collect (PRD-019). Each signature names one read-only capability of the script engine and its parameters; the server interprets what comes back. Edit this file to collect something new: the engines do not change. A query signature can only pick one of the queries written in the engine itself.

signatures.title: Windows edition, domain role and hardware
signatures.why: Whether the machine is a domain member, a server or a workstation decides which authentication and policy settings apply to it.

signatures.title: FIPS algorithm policy
signatures.why: With this policy on, Schannel, .NET and BitLocker refuse algorithms outside the FIPS-validated set; post-quantum algorithms arrive through this gate.

signatures.title: Secure Boot state
signatures.why: Secure Boot anchors the boot chain in firmware-held signature keys (RSA today); it is the first link of the machine's trust chain.

signatures.title: Virtualisation-based security, HVCI and Credential Guard
signatures.why: Credential Guard isolates Kerberos and NTLM secrets; HVCI protects the kernel's code integrity. Both change what an attacker on the box can reach.

signatures.title: Virtualisation-based security policy
signatures.why: The configured (as opposed to running) state of VBS and HVCI, as Group Policy or the registry set it.

signatures.title: TPM presence, version and readiness
signatures.why: A TPM holds BitLocker, Windows Hello and certificate keys in hardware. Those keys are RSA or ECC and cannot be swapped for post-quantum ones without new hardware or firmware.

signatures.title: BitLocker volumes and encryption method
signatures.why: Which volumes are encrypted, with which cipher (XTS-AES-128 or 256) and which protectors (TPM, PIN, recovery password).

signatures.title: BitLocker policy
signatures.why: The encryption method and the protectors Group Policy requires for new volumes.

signatures.title: Windows cryptographic stack versions
signatures.why: bcryptprimitives.dll is the FIPS-validated primitive module; schannel.dll is TLS; ncrypt.dll is key storage. Their versions say which Windows build's cryptography every program on the machine gets.

signatures.title: Cryptographic providers registered (CNG and legacy CAPI)
signatures.why: The key storage and algorithm providers programs can ask for: the Microsoft software and TPM providers, smart-card and HSM vendors' providers.

signatures.title: Legacy cryptographic service providers (CAPI)
signatures.why: Older programs use CAPI providers; which ones exist says what legacy key storage is in play.

signatures.title: Windows optional features enabled
signatures.why: SMB1, IIS, OpenSSH Server, Hyper-V, .NET 3.5 and similar features each bring their own protocols and cryptography.

signatures.title: TLS and SSL versions set for Windows (Schannel)
signatures.why: IIS, Remote Desktop, SQL Server and .NET use Schannel: a version explicitly enabled or disabled here applies to all of them.

signatures.title: Ciphers enabled or disabled for Schannel
signatures.why: RC4, 3DES, DES, NULL and AES toggles that apply to every Schannel connection on the machine.

signatures.title: Hashes enabled or disabled for Schannel
signatures.why: MD5 and SHA toggles for TLS handshakes and signatures.

signatures.title: Key exchange algorithms and minimum key sizes for Schannel
signatures.why: Diffie-Hellman and PKCS (RSA) key exchange toggles and the smallest key Schannel accepts (ClientMinKeyBitLength, ServerMinKeyBitLength).

signatures.title: Cipher suite order set locally (Schannel)
signatures.why: The order Windows offers and chooses suites in, when an administrator set it; empty means the Windows default order.

signatures.title: Cipher suite order set by Group Policy (Schannel)
signatures.why: A domain policy overrides the local order; this is where it lands.

signatures.title: Effective TLS cipher suites and curves (Schannel)
signatures.why: What Windows actually negotiates with, in order, after local settings, policy and defaults are combined: the list a scan of this machine's services would see.

signatures.title: Effective key exchange curves (Schannel)
signatures.why: The elliptic curves offered for ECDHE, in order; a post-quantum hybrid appears here when Windows ships one.

signatures.title: .NET Framework TLS settings (64-bit, 4.x)
signatures.why: SchUseStrongCrypto and SystemDefaultTlsVersions decide whether .NET Framework programs follow the operating system's TLS versions or stay on TLS 1.0.

signatures.title: .NET Framework TLS settings (32-bit, 4.x)
signatures.why: 32-bit .NET Framework programs read their own key; a machine can be fixed for one and not the other.

signatures.title: .NET Framework 2.0 and 3.5 TLS settings
signatures.why: Programs on the 2.0 runtime (3.5 included) have their own TLS switches; left alone they speak TLS 1.0.

signatures.title: .NET Framework release installed
signatures.why: The release number says which .NET Framework version (4.6.2 through 4.8.1) and so which TLS defaults programs get.

signatures.title: .NET (Core) runtimes installed
signatures.why: .NET 6, 8 and 9 use Schannel on Windows but carry their own TLS defaults and, from .NET 9, post-quantum APIs.

signatures.title: WinHTTP TLS versions
signatures.why: Services and scripts that use WinHTTP (Windows Update, PowerShell web cmdlets, many agents) negotiate the versions set here.

signatures.title: WinHTTP TLS versions (32-bit)
signatures.why: The 32-bit WinHTTP setting, read by 32-bit programs.

signatures.title: WinINet TLS versions (Internet Settings)
signatures.why: The SecureProtocols bit mask Internet Explorer, Edge legacy and WinINet-based programs use.

signatures.title: WinINet TLS versions set by policy
signatures.why: A Group Policy setting overrides the local SecureProtocols value.

signatures.title: Installed programs that bring their own cryptography
signatures.why: Libraries, runtimes, servers, VPN clients, smart-card middleware and HSM clients: each ships or depends on a cryptographic library of its own version.

signatures.title: Cryptographic libraries installed with applications
signatures.why: Applications that ship their own OpenSSL, NSS, libsodium or similar: their version decides which algorithms they can use, post-quantum ones included.

signatures.title: Language runtimes, servers and tools (executables with versions)
signatures.why: Python, Node, Go, Ruby, PHP, Java, .NET, PowerShell 7, web and database servers and SSH tools: each executable's version says which TLS stack and algorithms its programs get.

signatures.title: Java installations registered
signatures.why: Oracle and OpenJDK builds register their home and version here; a Java runtime brings its own TLS stack (JSSE) and trust store.

signatures.title: Java trust stores and security policy files present
signatures.why: Each JDK or JRE has a cacerts trust store and a java.security policy; a program trusts what its own Java trusts.

signatures.title: Java security policy (java.security)
signatures.why: jdk.tls.disabledAlgorithms, jdk.certpath.disabledAlgorithms, the provider order and the key store type decide what every Java program on this machine will negotiate and trust.

signatures.title: OpenSSH server policy (Windows)
signatures.why: The key exchange, ciphers, MACs, host key types and client key types the SSH server accepts, including post-quantum hybrids, and where its host keys are.

signatures.title: OpenSSH server host key types (Windows)
signatures.why: The public half of each host key says which signature algorithm clients verify the server with.

signatures.title: Algorithms the installed OpenSSH can use (Windows)
signatures.why: What the OpenSSH shipped with Windows is able to negotiate: whether the post-quantum hybrid key exchange (mlkem768x25519-sha256) is available at all.

signatures.title: Kerberos encryption types
signatures.why: Which enctypes this machine offers and accepts for Kerberos (AES-256, AES-128, RC4, DES); RC4 and DES are the usual legacy finding.

signatures.title: Kerberos encryption types (local setting)
signatures.why: The local Kerberos client setting, when no policy applies.

signatures.title: NTLM and LAN Manager authentication levels
signatures.why: LmCompatibilityLevel, NoLMHash and the NTLM restriction settings decide whether NTLMv1 or LM hashes can still be used.

signatures.title: NTLM minimum session security
signatures.why: NTLMMinClientSec and NTLMMinServerSec require NTLMv2 session security and 128-bit encryption.

signatures.title: SMB server signing, encryption and SMB1
signatures.why: Whether file shares require signing or encryption, and whether the SMB1 protocol is still enabled.

signatures.title: SMB client signing and guest access
signatures.why: Whether this machine signs SMB traffic it initiates and whether it allows insecure guest logons.

signatures.title: SMB server configuration (effective)
signatures.why: The running SMB server's settings: SMB1 on or off, signing, encryption and the ciphers it will use.

signatures.title: Netlogon secure channel
signatures.why: Whether the domain secure channel is signed, sealed and uses strong (AES) session keys.

signatures.title: LDAP signing and channel binding
signatures.why: The client's LDAP integrity requirement and, on a domain controller, the server's signing and channel-binding enforcement.

signatures.title: LDAP server signing (domain controller)
signatures.why: LDAPServerIntegrity and LdapEnforceChannelBinding on a domain controller decide whether unsigned LDAP binds are refused.

signatures.title: Remote Desktop security layer, encryption level and certificate
signatures.why: SecurityLayer 2 means TLS; MinEncryptionLevel 3 means 128-bit; UserAuthentication 1 means Network Level Authentication. The certificate hash is what clients verify.

signatures.title: Remote Desktop security set by policy
signatures.why: Group Policy values for the RDP security layer, encryption level and NLA override the local ones.

signatures.title: Certificates in the Windows stores
signatures.why: The personal, trusted root, intermediate, publisher, people, distrusted, Remote Desktop and web hosting stores, for the machine and the current user: what this machine trusts and what it can present.

signatures.title: Key storage provider of each personal certificate
signatures.why: Whether a certificate's private key is in the TPM (Microsoft Platform Crypto Provider), in the software key storage provider, on a smart card, or in a legacy CSP: hardware-bound keys cannot be replaced by post-quantum ones in place.

signatures.title: Certificate auto-enrolment policy
signatures.why: Whether this machine and its users enrol for certificates from Active Directory Certificate Services automatically.

signatures.title: Active Directory Certificate Services on this machine
signatures.why: A certificate authority running here is the issuer of the fleet's certificates; its key algorithm sets the fleet's floor.

signatures.title: Encrypting File System algorithm
signatures.why: The algorithm EFS encrypts files with (AES-256 by default, 3DES or DESX on older policy).

signatures.title: HTTP.sys TLS certificate bindings
signatures.why: Which certificate each HTTPS port served by HTTP.sys (IIS, WinRM, many Windows services) presents, and from which store: the binding of a key to a listening service.

signatures.title: IIS installed
signatures.why: Internet Information Services serves TLS through Schannel; its presence makes the Schannel and HTTP.sys settings above those of a web server.

signatures.title: IIS site bindings (HTTPS)
signatures.why: Each HTTPS binding names the certificate hash and store a site presents.

signatures.title: WinRM listeners
signatures.why: Remote management listeners on HTTP and HTTPS, and the certificate an HTTPS listener presents.

signatures.title: Listening services and the cryptographic libraries they loaded
signatures.why: Each listening TCP or UDP socket with its process, executable and the TLS and key-storage DLLs in that process (schannel, ncrypt, a bundled OpenSSL, NSS): what is actually running with which cryptography.

signatures.title: Kernel and architecture
signatures.why: The kernel version decides which in-kernel cryptography (dm-crypt, kTLS, WireGuard, IPsec) and which TPM and random-number support exist.

signatures.title: Kernel FIPS mode
signatures.why: With fips_enabled=1 the kernel, OpenSSL, GnuTLS, NSS and OpenSSH restrict themselves to FIPS-approved algorithms.

signatures.title: System-wide crypto policy
signatures.why: On RHEL, Fedora, CentOS and derivatives one policy (DEFAULT, FUTURE, FIPS, LEGACY) sets the floor for OpenSSL, GnuTLS, NSS, OpenSSH, Java and Kerberos at once.

signatures.title: Crypto policy and FIPS mode as reported
signatures.why: What update-crypto-policies and fips-mode-setup say is in force, which can differ from the file when a change has not been applied.

signatures.title: Crypto policy back ends (OpenSSL, GnuTLS, NSS, OpenSSH, Java, Kerberos)
signatures.why: The generated per-library policy files are what each library actually reads.

signatures.title: CPU cryptographic instructions
signatures.why: AES-NI, SHA extensions and carry-less multiply decide whether AES-GCM and SHA-2 run in hardware; RDRAND and RDSEED feed the random generator.

signatures.title: Kernel crypto API algorithms
signatures.why: The algorithms the kernel's crypto API has registered, used by dm-crypt, IPsec, kTLS, WireGuard and file-system encryption.

signatures.title: Kernel modules for cryptography, TPM and tunnels
signatures.why: Which acceleration, disk-encryption, TPM, TLS-offload and VPN modules are loaded.

signatures.title: TPM presence and version
signatures.why: A TPM anchors disk encryption, measured boot and (through tpm2-pkcs11 or the OpenSSL TPM2 provider) keys; its keys are RSA or ECC.

signatures.title: Encrypted block devices (dm-crypt, LUKS)
signatures.why: Which devices are encrypted volumes or LUKS containers; the cipher is in the LUKS header, which only root can read.

signatures.title: Encrypted volumes set up at boot (crypttab)
signatures.why: The volumes unlocked at boot, with the options (cipher, key file location, TPM2 or FIDO2 enrolment) each uses.

signatures.title: Secure Boot state
signatures.why: Whether the firmware verifies the boot loader's signature; the kernel then enforces module signing.

signatures.title: Password hashing algorithm
signatures.why: ENCRYPT_METHOD and the pam_unix options decide whether account passwords are hashed with yescrypt, SHA-512, SHA-256 or MD5.

signatures.title: Installed cryptographic packages, servers and runtimes
signatures.why: OpenSSL, GnuTLS, NSS, libgcrypt, OpenSSH, Java, Python, Node, Go, web, mail, database and VPN servers, PKCS#11 and TPM tools, with versions: the version decides which algorithms each can use, post-quantum ones included.

signatures.title: Cryptographic shared libraries on disk
signatures.why: Libraries bundled with applications under /opt, /srv, /usr/local or /var/lib, beside the distribution's own: each is a version to track.

signatures.title: OpenSSL version and build
signatures.why: The system OpenSSL's exact version, build flags, configuration directory and module directory; 3.5 brings ML-KEM and ML-DSA.

signatures.title: OpenSSL providers loaded
signatures.why: Which providers the system configuration activates (default, legacy, FIPS, OQS, PKCS#11, TPM2): the FIPS provider restricts, the OQS provider adds post-quantum algorithms.

signatures.title: OpenSSL provider modules installed
signatures.why: A FIPS, OQS, PKCS#11, TPM2 or legacy provider module on disk can be activated by configuration; its presence is the first sign.

signatures.title: Key encapsulation algorithms the installed OpenSSL offers
signatures.why: ML-KEM-512, -768 and -1024 listed here means the library can do post-quantum key exchange; absent means an upgrade is needed first.

signatures.title: Signature algorithms the installed OpenSSL offers
signatures.why: ML-DSA and SLH-DSA listed here means the library can sign and verify post-quantum certificates.

signatures.title: OpenSSL default cipher suites
signatures.why: The suites the DEFAULT cipher string yields for this build and configuration: the starting point of every program that does not set its own.

signatures.title: GnuTLS version
signatures.why: GnuTLS serves Exim, many GNOME programs, rsyslog and others; its version decides their algorithms.

signatures.title: GnuPG version and algorithms
signatures.why: GnuPG signs packages, commits and mail; the algorithms it lists are what it can create and verify.

signatures.title: curl and its TLS backend
signatures.why: curl's TLS backend (OpenSSL, GnuTLS, rustls) and the libssh2 and Kerberos libraries it links are what scripts and agents on the machine use.

signatures.title: wget and its TLS backend
signatures.why: wget links OpenSSL or GnuTLS; its version decides what downloads will negotiate.

signatures.title: Java version and location
signatures.why: Which Java runs by default, and from where; the JDK version decides whether ML-KEM (JDK 24) and ML-DSA are available to Java programs.

signatures.title: Java trust stores and security policy files present
signatures.why: Each JDK's cacerts trust store and java.security policy, including Debian's shared one.

signatures.title: Java security policy (java.security)
signatures.why: jdk.tls.disabledAlgorithms, jdk.certpath.disabledAlgorithms, the provider order and the key store type decide what every Java program on this machine negotiates and trusts.

signatures.title: Python and the OpenSSL it links
signatures.why: Python's ssl module uses the OpenSSL it was built against, which may differ from the system's (pyenv, conda, containers).

signatures.title: Node.js and its bundled OpenSSL
signatures.why: Node statically bundles OpenSSL; its version, not the system's, decides what Node programs negotiate.

signatures.title: Go toolchain version
signatures.why: Go programs use Go's own TLS stack; Go 1.24 negotiates X25519MLKEM768 by default.

signatures.title: Ruby and the OpenSSL it links
signatures.why: Ruby's openssl extension reports the library it was built against.

signatures.title: PHP and the OpenSSL it links
signatures.why: PHP's openssl extension reports the library it was built against.

signatures.title: .NET runtimes installed
signatures.why: .NET on Linux uses the system OpenSSL; the runtime version decides its TLS defaults and post-quantum APIs.

signatures.title: OpenSSL system-wide configuration
signatures.why: The minimum protocol, cipher string, groups, signature algorithms, and the providers the configuration activates (FIPS, legacy, OQS): the starting point of every program using the system OpenSSL.

signatures.title: GnuTLS system configuration
signatures.why: The system-wide priority string and overrides every GnuTLS program starts from.

signatures.title: NSS system policy
signatures.why: The policy file Firefox, Thunderbird, curl (NSS builds) and others read for allowed algorithms and versions.

signatures.title: OpenSSH server policy as written
signatures.why: The key exchange, ciphers, MACs, host key types and client key types the SSH server accepts, including post-quantum hybrids, and the host keys and includes it uses.

signatures.title: OpenSSH server policy as effective
signatures.why: What sshd itself reports after defaults, includes and the crypto policy are applied: the algorithms a client connecting to this machine is actually offered.

signatures.title: OpenSSH client policy
signatures.why: What outbound SSH from this machine will offer: key exchange, ciphers, MACs, host key and key types.

signatures.title: Algorithms the installed OpenSSH can use
signatures.why: What the installed OpenSSH is able to negotiate: whether the post-quantum hybrid key exchanges (mlkem768x25519-sha256, sntrup761x25519-sha512) exist at all.

signatures.title: OpenSSH version and the OpenSSL it links
signatures.why: ssh -V names the OpenSSH release and the OpenSSL it was built with.

signatures.title: OpenSSH server host key types
signatures.why: The public half of each host key says which signature algorithm clients verify the server with.

signatures.title: OpenSSH host key sizes and fingerprints
signatures.why: ssh-keygen -l reports each host key's size (bits) and SHA-256 fingerprint: a 2048-bit RSA host key is a finding of its own.

signatures.title: nginx TLS configuration
signatures.why: ssl_protocols, ssl_ciphers, ssl_ecdh_curve, ssl_prefer_server_ciphers, stapling, tickets and the certificate each server block presents.

signatures.title: nginx version and the OpenSSL it was built with
signatures.why: nginx -V names the OpenSSL version nginx was compiled against and the one it runs with.

signatures.title: Apache httpd TLS configuration
signatures.why: SSLProtocol, SSLCipherSuite, SSLHonorCipherOrder, SSLOpenSSLConfCmd and the certificate each virtual host presents.

signatures.title: Apache httpd version and build
signatures.why: httpd -V names the server version and whether it was built with OpenSSL.

signatures.title: HAProxy TLS configuration
signatures.why: ssl-default-bind-ciphers, ssl-min-ver, tune.ssl settings and the certificates bound to each frontend.

signatures.title: HAProxy version and the OpenSSL it runs with
signatures.why: haproxy -vv names the HAProxy release and the OpenSSL it was built with and runs with.

signatures.title: Postfix TLS configuration
signatures.why: smtpd_tls_* and smtp_tls_* decide what mail in and out of this machine is encrypted with and which certificate it presents.

signatures.title: Postfix TLS settings in force
signatures.why: postconf -n lists the non-default settings Postfix runs with, which can differ from main.cf when a change has not been reloaded.

signatures.title: Dovecot TLS configuration
signatures.why: ssl_min_protocol, ssl_cipher_list, ssl_prefer_server_ciphers and the certificate the IMAP and POP services present.

signatures.title: Dovecot TLS settings in force
signatures.why: doveconf -n lists the settings Dovecot runs with.

signatures.title: Exim TLS configuration
signatures.why: tls_advertise_hosts, tls_require_ciphers and the certificate Exim presents.

signatures.title: PostgreSQL TLS configuration
signatures.why: ssl, ssl_min_protocol_version, ssl_ciphers, ssl_ecdh_curve and the certificate the database presents.

signatures.title: MySQL and MariaDB TLS configuration
signatures.why: tls_version, ssl-cipher, require_secure_transport and the certificate the database presents.

signatures.title: OpenLDAP TLS configuration (client and server)
signatures.why: TLS_CACERT, TLS_REQCERT, TLSCipherSuite and TLSProtocolMin for directory connections in and out of this machine.

signatures.title: Samba protocol, signing and encryption settings
signatures.why: server min protocol, smb encrypt, server signing, ntlm auth and the LDAP and TLS settings of a Samba file or domain server.

params.match: ^[[:space:]]*(server min protocol|server max protocol|client min protocol|client max protocol|smb encrypt|server smb encrypt|client smb encrypt|server signing|client signing|ntlm auth|lanman auth|raw NTLMv2 auth|tls enabled|tls priority|tls certfile|tls cafile|ldap ssl|ldap server require strong auth|client ldap sasl wrapping|kerberos encryption types)[[:space:]]*=

signatures.title: Samba settings in force
signatures.why: testparm -s prints the settings Samba runs with, defaults resolved.

params.match: min protocol|max protocol|smb encrypt|signing|ntlm auth|lanman auth|tls |ldap ssl|kerberos encryption

signatures.title: BIND DNSSEC and DNS-over-TLS settings
signatures.why: dnssec-validation, dnssec-policy and tls blocks: DNSSEC signing keys are RSA or ECDSA and have their own migration path.

signatures.title: BIND version and the OpenSSL it links
signatures.why: named -V names the BIND release and its OpenSSL.

signatures.title: Kubernetes API server TLS flags
signatures.why: --tls-min-version, --tls-cipher-suites and the certificate, CA and service-account signing key files the control plane uses.

signatures.title: systemd-resolved DNS-over-TLS and DNSSEC
signatures.why: Whether the machine's stub resolver encrypts and validates DNS.

signatures.title: chrony Network Time Security
signatures.why: NTS authenticates time with TLS; unauthenticated time undermines certificate validity checks.

signatures.title: OpenVPN cipher, authentication and TLS settings
signatures.why: data-ciphers, auth, tls-version-min, tls-cipher, tls-crypt and the certificate and CA each tunnel uses (inline key blocks are never copied).

signatures.title: OpenVPN version and its OpenSSL
signatures.why: openvpn --version names the release and the OpenSSL it links.

signatures.title: IPsec (strongSwan, libreswan) proposals
signatures.why: ike and esp proposals, key exchange version and authentication method of each connection: where IKEv2 post-quantum hybrids will appear.

signatures.title: strongSwan or libreswan version
signatures.why: The IKE daemon's version decides which proposals it supports.

signatures.title: WireGuard interfaces up
signatures.why: WireGuard uses Curve25519, ChaCha20-Poly1305 and BLAKE2s, fixed by the protocol; an interface present means that cryptography is in use. Its configuration files hold keys and are never read.

signatures.title: stunnel TLS settings
signatures.why: The protocol versions, ciphers, curves and certificates each stunnel service wraps a plain connection in.

signatures.title: stunnel version and its OpenSSL
signatures.why: stunnel -version names the release and the OpenSSL it links.

signatures.title: Kerberos encryption types (krb5.conf, kdc.conf)
signatures.why: permitted, default ticket and default TGS enctypes, allow_weak_crypto and a KDC's supported enctypes and master key type.

signatures.title: Certificates in the trust store and in service folders
signatures.why: What the machine trusts (system and locally added anchors) and what its services present (web, mail, Kubernetes, container, VPN folders): the public halves only.

signatures.title: PKCS#11 modules registered (p11-kit)
signatures.why: Smart cards, HSMs, TPM2 and SoftHSM reach OpenSSL, GnuTLS, NSS and OpenSSH through these modules.

signatures.title: SoftHSM configuration
signatures.why: A software HSM holding keys for tests or services; where its tokens live and how objects are stored.

signatures.title: cryptsetup version
signatures.why: The disk-encryption tool's version decides LUKS2, Argon2 and the ciphers it offers.

signatures.title: Listening services and the cryptographic libraries they loaded
signatures.why: Each listening TCP or UDP socket with its process, executable and the TLS and crypto libraries mapped into that process (libssl, libcrypto, libgnutls, nss3, libsodium): what is actually running with which cryptography. Go and Rust programs carry their own and show none.
